cells.tense: This practice has been yours long enough that the doing has gone quiet, and the quiet is where the view sharpens.
cells.ask: Hand one unfinished piece to someone who hasn't seen it and listen for what their eyes catch that yours have stopped registering.
cells.core:
The bench is a place you return to, not a task you push through, and the repetition has thinned the noise down to a cleaner view of what matters. Because the whole shape sits in front of you, you keep finding the next small thing — not because anything's wrong, just because the view is that clear. The work gets a little truer each pass, and you can feel the difference in your hands more than in your head.

That kind of steady attention is doing more for you than the work itself. When someone else looks at one unfinished piece without your history, they catch what you've stopped noticing. It doesn't dilute the practice. A second set of eyes gives the view something to sharpen against, and what comes back sharpens both of you.
cells.sheetLine: Your steady attention keeps the view clear, and a second pair of eyes sharpens it further.
cells.verb: Return to the same work until it deepens
cells.place: Standing back and seeing how all the pieces fit

cells.tense: You're already living in the finished version of this, and you're trying to drag the work up to meet it.
cells.ask: Set twenty minutes and touch only what's actually in front of you, nothing further ahead.
cells.core:
The bench is where you're steady and the work gets better for it — that part is real and it's yours. But right now you've got a finished picture in your head the work can't match yet, and your attention is on the gap instead of the wood. The pushing crowds out the slower feedback that got you here.

The craft hasn't failed you. You've just stopped hearing what the work is saying at this stage, because you're arguing with it about where it should be. Put the finished version down. Work on what's there. When the work speaks again, the next step shows itself without force, and the process can be enjoyed instead of defended.
cells.sheetLine: You're racing the work toward a finish it hasn't reached, and missing what it's telling you now.
cells.growth: Growth vector: Celebration — let the unfinished version be enough for today.

cells.tense: You're holding your read of the whole thing privately, and the practice has gone quiet alongside it.
cells.ask: Say one clear thing you actually see about the whole situation, then do one task today that follows straight from it.
cells.core:
Standing back and catching the shape of everything — that ability hasn't gone anywhere. It's still yours, and it shows when you look at the whole board without adding anything to it. What changed is that you've stopped saying it out loud, and the practice has settled around that quiet. The work isn't asking for more thought. It's asking you to name what you see and move.

When someone asks what you think, you give them a clear answer. Same muscle as the craft: look at the whole, say what's true, do the next thing. One honest sentence and one small task that comes from it. The view returns as you use it, and using it is the whole of the ask.
cells.sheetLine: You can still see the shape of it. Say what you see and begin again.

cells.tense: The choosing is already happening and you're the one doing it, but you describe the effort like it landed on you from somewhere.
cells.ask: Before your next session, say one sentence out loud naming what you're choosing to work on and one reason it matters.
cells.core:
The steady return to the bench is real, and it's yours — nobody handed you this practice. It's the kind of work that makes things around it hold together, and people feel that reliability even when the hours behind it stay out of sight. But somewhere along the way the reasons went quiet, and you keep your own reasons for the work out of the conversation, sometimes out of your own head. The silence makes the momentum feel like a current you're caught in.

What's going well is that the work itself is honest. It can take a plain sentence. Say what you're doing and why it matters in your own voice, and the effort stops feeling like something you owe and starts feeling like something you picked. One sentence, out loud, before the next session.
cells.sheetLine: This work is yours. Name what it's for in your own voice.

attempts.check: The weakest claim is that the person's craft has become a way of seeing everything, which the record doesn't establish — the card speaks only to one sustained practice, not to the whole of someone's perception. A reader could reasonably say 'no, the work is just work; the pattern-recognition is something else.' The asks all survive that objection, because each one names a concrete act that would teach the person something about their own relationship to the work whether or not the reading is right. The sentence that serves the writer is the closing line of the Too Little cell — it's a nice turn of phrase, and the person gets a prettier sentence than they get a usable one; it should be replaced with something plainer.
